Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Weapons): Weapons or objects used as weapons
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening accident, weapon-related visual triggers are hard to reconcile unless the accident specifically involved assaultive circumstances, which is not implied by the trauma type. This item suggests an interpersonal violence context rather than an accident context.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
issues.explanation: Sudden movements by others putting her immediately on guard fits a threat profile centered on interpersonal attack. Combined with weapon triggers, it pulls the presentation toward assault-related PTSD rather than PTSD following an accident, creating a cross-node mismatch with the stated trauma type.

vignette:
Adaeze is an eighty-year-old Ghanaian-American midwife who has spent more than five decades guiding new life into the world. She has been married for fifty-three years, and until fourteen months ago her days were organized around the rhythms of a small birth center where she still consulted part-time, her experience valued by younger colleagues who sought her counsel. That life changed on a Tuesday afternoon in early spring when the sedan she was driving was struck broadside by a delivery truck that ran a red light. The impact was instantaneous and total: her door caved inward, the car spun and came to rest against a concrete divider, and Adaeze found herself pinned, unable to open her door, the windows sealed, the smell of hot metal filling the cabin while the first sirens rose in the distance. She was conscious throughout the forty minutes it took for rescuers to cut her free. She sustained fractures to her pelvis and left wrist, injuries that required surgery and months of rehabilitation, and that have left her with a persistent limp and limited grip strength in the hand she has used to deliver thousands of babies.

In the weeks following her discharge, Adaeze began to notice that certain things in the ordinary world reached inside her and pulled the accident back. The sound of an ambulance siren - unavoidable in the neighborhood near the birth center - would stop her mid-sentence, her body flooding with the same trapped, airless dread she had felt inside the crumpled car. Seeing photographs of accident scenes on the evening news, or passing the intersection where it happened on the way to her daughter's house, produced the same sudden collapse of past and present. Confined spaces became almost unbearable: the elevator at her cardiologist's office, a small examination room with the door closed, the back seat of her son-in-law's car when the child locks were engaged. Each of these triggers reliably activated a state of acute physical alarm - her heart racing, her senses sharpened to an almost painful acuity, her body scanning the environment for the next impact. She began sleeping with the bedroom door open and a lamp on, but even so she lay awake for hours, her ears tuned to every sound in the house, startling violently when the refrigerator cycled or a car passed outside. The hypervigilance that the accident had switched on did not switch off at night, and the sleeplessness in turn left her raw and easily frightened through the following day, so that ordinary sounds she would once have ignored - a dropped tray at the birth center, a colleague's raised voice - sent her lurching from her chair.

What has perhaps done the most damage, though, is what Adaeze tells herself about all of this. The persistent alarm state, the nights without sleep, the way her body refuses to settle, have fed a set of convictions that have grown harder with each passing month. She has come to believe, with a certainty she finds shameful, that another woman - a more alert woman, a younger woman, a woman less distracted by the small fatigue of age - would not have been in that intersection at that moment. The thought arrives unbidden, and when it does, it sharpens every trigger: the siren outside the birth center becomes not just a reminder of the accident but evidence of her own culpability, and confined spaces feel not merely dangerous but deserved. She is equally certain that her body has been permanently altered in ways that cannot be undone - the limp, the weakened hand - and she interprets these physical facts as confirmation that her life as she knew it is simply over. That belief, once settled, makes the world feel saturated with threat: she monitors exits in every room she enters, she flinches at sounds, she cannot sleep. The loop has become self-sealing. The vigilance exhausts her; the exhaustion confirms that she is diminished; the diminishment sends her back to the triggers with even less resilience than before.

Adaeze finally sought help after she was unable to assist at a birth for the first time in her career - she froze in the doorway of the delivery room when the door swung shut behind her, and had to be helped to a chair in the corridor. What she most fears is that she will never work again. What she most hopes, though she says it quietly, is that someone can tell her the woman she was before the accident has not entirely disappeared.
